newsitem.title: UK: Feb 5 last likely date for UK pre-poll rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Feb 5 last likely date for UK pre-poll rate rise.

text.p: The next UK monetary policy meeting on February 5 is probably the Chancellor's last chance to raise interest rates before the election, a move he appears increasingly reluctant to make, economists said.

The unpopular Conservative government is unlikely to risk a rate rise any closer to polling day, even though the impact of such a move on the real economy would not be felt until well after the election.
The about-turn in the outlook for rates appeared to sink into the currency markets overnight as overseas investors bailed out of sterling following a sharp fall in December retail sales.
"I think if we go beyond the February 5 meeting, it's quite hard to see a rate rise taking place after that," said Merrill Lynch economist Ian Stewart.

Chancellor Kenneth Clarke last raised interest rates on October 30 by 25 basis points to 6.0 percent. He passed up opportunities to do so again in December and January, convincing many economists that his mind is made up.
"It is very likely indeed that Clarke won't put rates up before the election," said CIBC Wood Gundy chief economist David Coleman.
"He made his position very clear last week and if anything, the figures we've had since then have reinforced that decision."
Clarke left interest rates on hold after his monetary meeting with Bank of England Governor Eddie George last Wednesday, citing sterling's strength as a key factor.
George publicly rejected that argument on Monday this week, warning that there were real dangers in using sterling's strength as an excuse not to tighten policy.
Economists said the sudden slide in sterling overnight will do little to affect Clarke's argument.
"We need a much more sustained fall in the currency for Clarke to change his view or, perhaps more importantly, for the market to think he will," said Coleman.
The government's reluctance to raise rates ahead of the election, which must be held within the next four months, stems from the knock-on effect on mortgage rates.
In a nation where two-thirds of households are home-owners, and around 85 percent of them have a variable rate mortgage, a rise in interest rates is highly politically sensitive.
But Rob Thomas, housing analyst at UBS, said the impact of a small rise in mortgage rates on the average household would actually be minimal.
"There is a certain psychological impact from raising rates, but a quarter point increase is chicken feed...it's difficult to notice," he said.
Mortgage rates would definitely rise following a base rate increase, Thomas said. "The pressure for them to go up is so strong, they will probably rise at some point even if base rates don't."
He estimates mortgage rates will end the year around 8.0 percent, up from their current 7.1 percent.
"But in the run up to an election, the government doesn't want to see that happen. Clarke would be loath to put up rates after February."
Stewart of Merrill Lynch said an increase in rates would likely affect consumer confidence.

"Consumer confidence fell back somewhat in December, and one possible explanation is that we saw a rate rise at the end of October," he said. "Certainly at least with the Nationwide building society, it fed through to December mortgages."
"I don't think it's a massive issue, but they would rather not raise rates."
